scenario_stem:
Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by the Ferreira family in Country X. It employs 42 workers making premium boxed chocolates at its Bellport factory. Last year it sold 1.4 million boxes at $8 each, earning revenue of $11.2 million. Recently, complaints about broken pralines have risen to 240 a month, and 18% of boxes failed final inspection in May.

Managing Director Carla Ferreira must decide between two options before the Christmas gifting range ships in 10 weeks. Option A is quality control: adding an end-of-line inspection team to catch faulty boxes before dispatch, costing $60,000 a year. Option B is quality assurance: building checks into every production stage and training 30 workers to inspect recipes, enrobing and packaging, costing $95,000 to set up but cutting rework.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'quality assurance'.
questions.model_answer: Quality assurance is a system of building quality into every stage of production, from raw materials to dispatch, so that faults are prevented rather than just detected [2].

knowledge_max_2: Quality is built into every stage of production
Faults are prevented rather than just detected

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why quality is important to Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd.
questions.model_answer: First, quality is important because high-quality chocolates satisfy customers and build loyalty [k]. With complaints already at 240 a month, fixing quality would protect the Christmas gifting range and encourage shoppers to reorder Hazelmere boxes [app]. Second, quality is important because poor quality wastes resources [k]. The 18% of boxes failing final inspection contain wasted ingredients and labour, so improving quality lowers costs and protects the $11.2 million revenue [app].

knowledge_max_2: Quality builds customer satisfaction and loyalty
Quality reduces waste, rework and costs
application_max_2: Reference to 240 complaints a month / Christmas gifting range
Reference to 18% failing final inspection / $11.2 million revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd might face if it introduces quality control (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, quality control checks products at the end of production, so faults are only detected after costs have been added [k]. With 18% of boxes already failing final inspection, even a larger inspection team would simply find more faulty boxes without stopping them being made, raising rework and scrap [app]. This would increase costs rather than remove the root cause of the defect problem, squeezing profit [an]. Second, quality control adds a permanent wage bill for inspectors [k]. The extra team costs $60,000 a year on top of existing wages for 42 workers, and that money cannot also train 30 production workers [app]. The ongoing expense reduces funds available for improvements such as Option B, limiting long-term competitiveness [an].

knowledge_max_2: Quality control checks at the end of production; faults detected late
Quality control adds a permanent staffing cost
application_max_2: Reference to 18% failing final inspection
Reference to $60,000 a year / 42 workers / 30 workers to train
analysis_max_2: Chain from late detection to rework and scrap to higher costs and squeezed profit
Chain from inspector wages to fewer funds for training to weaker long-term competitiveness

questions.question_text: Do you think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should introduce quality assurance (Option B) rather than quality control (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A, quality control, would catch faulty boxes at the end of the line, protecting customers quickly before dispatch [k]. At $60,000 a year it is cheaper up front and would visibly cut complaints during the 10 weeks before the Christmas gifting range ships [app]. This rapid protection is valuable given the reputation risk at peak season [an]. However, Option B, quality assurance, prevents defects at every stage rather than detecting them afterwards [k]. Training 30 of the 42 workers to check recipes, enrobing and packaging costs $95,000 to set up, but it attacks the rework behind the 18% failure rate directly [app]. Preventing faults earlier reduces wasted ingredients, rework and complaints, protecting Hazelmere's $11.2 million revenue more sustainably than end-of-line checks [an]. Overall, I think Hazelmere Chocolates Ltd should choose Option B [eval] because prevention is cheaper than failure: the $95,000 is less than two years of Option A at $60,000 a year, after which Option B is cheaper and errors fall further [eval].

Quality assurance prevents faults at every stage

scenario_stem:
Driftwood Toy Co is a private limited company owned by Daniel Reyes, designing wooden trains and puzzles at its Ashfield workshop in Country X. It employs 68 workers and exports toys to 6 countries through independent shops. Last year it produced 900,000 units selling at an average of $8 each, earning $7.2 million. Export returns caused by a paint defect reached 5% of shipments, and one retailer threatened to cancel a $400,000 order.

Daniel must decide in 8 weeks, before the retailer's order review. Option A: introduce Total Quality Management across the business, making every worker responsible for quality with weekly improvement meetings and a suggestion scheme, costing $30,000 in training. Option B: keep the current system of 4 end-of-line inspectors checking finished toys, which adds no new cost but leaves export returns unchanged.

scenario_stem:
Timberline Joinery is a partnership owned by brothers Adam and Eli Kovac, manufacturing fitted wardrobes and kitchens at its Kilndown workshop in Country X. It employs 25 workers, producing 1,150 units last year and earning revenue of $3.6 million. Rework caused by finish flaws affects 9% of units, and a national housebuilder has offered a contract worth $900,000 a year if consistent quality can be evidenced by independent assessment.

The partners must decide in 6 weeks, before signing the housebuilder contract. Option A: pay $70,000 for an external quality audit and a 12-month certification, renewable each year, proving standards to buyers and reducing the need to prove quality for every new order. Option B: keep weekend in-house checks costing $5,000, with no external validation and no proof to show the housebuilder, but immediate savings.

Securing this independent approval makes the $900,000 contract far more likely, lifting revenue by a quarter [an]. Second, external audits identify weaknesses in production processes [k]. Auditors would examine how the 25 workers prepare, fit and finish each unit and flag the flaws causing 9% rework [app]. scenario_stem:

It employs 110 workers at its Rivergate factory and knitted 600,000 garments last year, selling at an average of $15 each for revenue of $9 million. Complaints and returns over stitching faults reached 12,000 garments last quarter, and its main overseas customer, a fashion retail group taking 60% of output, has demanded a corrective action plan.

Managing Director Sara Okafor must act within 5 weeks, ahead of the retailer's supplier audit. Option A: hire 6 more inspectors for $54,000 a year to double-check finished garments. Option B: introduce quality assurance at every stage, from yarn inspection to knitting, linking and pressing, with retraining for all 110 workers, costing $80,000 as a one-off.

scenario_stem:
Bramblewick Honey is a sole trader business owned by Yusuf Rahman on his 22-hectare farm in Country X, bottling honey from 80 hives delivered weekly. He produces 36,000 jars a year sold at $5 each, giving revenue of $180,000, through farmers' markets and 14 local shops. A supermarket chain wants to list his honey in 30 stores but requires batch testing before each delivery, following two complaints of incorrectly blended honey.

Yusuf must decide within 4 weeks. Option A: pay a laboratory to test every delivery batch for $8,000 a year, a quality control approach of checking finished jars. Option B: buy a refractometer and jarring equipment for $6,000 as a one-off and introduce quality assurance checklists for extraction, straining and jarring at each stage.

questions.model_answer: First, higher quality would help secure the new contract [k]. Listing in 30 stores would massively expand sales beyond his 14 local shops, multiplying market reach [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. With complaints of incorrectly blended honey already recorded, proving reliable jars to the supermarket would earn repeat, larger orders [app].

questions.model_answer: First, testing finished batches detects faults but does not prevent them [k]. Blending and straining errors would already have happened by the time the laboratory approves a batch, so jars of incorrectly blended honey could still slip through to the 30 stores [app]. A rejected batch would destroy honey he has already paid to produce and jar [an]. Second, the laboratory fee is a permanent annual cost [k]. Paying $8,000 a year cuts into the $180,000 revenue from jars sold at $5 each, eroding his small margin [app]. Over two years the $16,000 total exceeds the $6,000 cost of Option B's equipment [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Yusuf Rahman should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $6,000 once and introduces quality assurance checklists at extraction, straining and jarring, preventing faults at source [k]. Over two years Option A costs $16,000 against $6,000 for Option B, leaving more cash for Yusuf to fund growth [an]. The $8,000 a year fee is also ongoing, and a failed batch wastes both the fee and the production cost of that batch [an]. Overall, I think Yusuf should choose Option B [eval], provided the supermarket accepts documented QA procedures: it prevents faults, saves $10,000 over two years and builds lasting capability [eval].

Overall, I think Ferndale Tiles should choose Option B [eval], because it prevents faults permanently and costs less, unless the hotel group rejects uncertified systems, in which case Option A is a necessary $45,000 investment to secure the $600,000 contract [eval].

scenario_stem:
Amberleigh Dairies is a private limited company processing 90,000 litres of milk a week at its Kilndown site in Country X, supplying pasteurised milk and yoghurt to 40 shops and 8 cafes. It employs 26 staff and earned revenue of $2.9 million last year. Three deliveries were found to contain sour milk last month, 2% of yoghurt pots came in below weight, and its largest customer, a 10-shop chain, is reviewing its supplier list.

The owners must decide within 5 weeks. Option A: hire 2 inspectors to test finished batches at packing, a quality control approach costing $30,000 a year. Option B: install quality assurance controls, covering temperature and time checks in pasteurisation, calibrated filling machines and hygiene training, costing $40,000 as a one-off.

Sour milk in three deliveries last month risks making customers ill, which could lead to fines, product seizures and prosecution [app]. Second, quality protects customer relationships and sales [k]. The 10-shop chain, its largest customer, is reviewing suppliers, and repeated faults would push it to switch to a rival dairy [app].

questions.model_answer: First, checking finished batches detects faults only after they occur [k]. Pasteurisation errors and underweight filling happen upstream, so inspectors would find but not fix the 2% below-weight pots [app]. Scrapped pots waste milk already processed, raising costs [an]. Second, sampling at packing can miss faulty items in a large batch [k]. With 90,000 litres processed weekly, sour milk could still slip through in untested pots reaching 40 shops and 8 cafes [app]. One case of food poisoning could cost the dairy its 10-shop chain and permanently damage its reputation [an].

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberleigh Dairies should choose quality assurance (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $40,000 once and prevents faults at source: pasteurisation temperature and time checks, calibrated filling machines and hygiene training remove the causes of sour milk and below-weight pots [k]. Preventing failures before packing protects the 40 shops, 8 cafes and the 10-shop chain whose review is due within 5 weeks [app]. Over two years Option B costs $40,000 while Option A costs $60,000, so prevention is both safer and cheaper [an]. However, Option A hires 2 inspectors for $30,000 a year and starts immediately, giving early warning on every finished batch as an independent checkpoint [k]. But Option A recurs at $60,000 over two years, detects rather than prevents, and leaves pasteurisation faults unchecked at source [app]. A single missed batch could still end the 10-shop chain relationship, threatening $2.9 million of revenue [an]. Overall, I think Amberleigh Dairies should choose Option B [eval] because it addresses root causes, costs $20,000 less over two years and directly defends the largest customer contract [eval].

scenario_stem:
Osprey Electronics is a private limited company assembling smart-home control panels for property developers at its Eastholme production unit in Country X. It employs 64 workers and produced 24,000 units last year at $250 each, earning $6 million. Bench tests show 7% of units fail, costing $180,000 a year in rework, and warranty claims are rising. A developer considering an order of 8,000 panels wants evidence of a defect-reduction plan.

The owners must decide in 6 weeks before the developer decides on the order. Option A: add tester overtime for $25,000 a year to clear the inspection backlog, keeping the current end-of-line quality control. Option B: adopt Total Quality Management over 12 months, forming cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and a supplier quality programme, costing $85,000.

questions.question_text: Identify two costs a business might incur to improve quality.
questions.model_answer: Installing inspection and testing equipment is one cost of improving quality [1]. Training workers to check their own work at each stage is another cost [1]. [2]

Training costs for staff on quality checks

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why reducing the failure rate matters to Osprey Electronics.
questions.model_answer: First, a lower failure rate cuts rework costs [k]. Failures already cost $180,000 a year, so fixing processes would release funds for wages and materials [app]. Second, fewer defects build customer trust and win orders [k]. The developer weighing an 8,000-panel order, worth $2 million at $250 each, will favour a supplier with a credible defect-reduction plan [app].

Lower defects build trust and help win orders
application_max_2: Reference to $180,000 a year rework cost

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of adopting Total Quality Management (Option B) at Osprey Electronics.
questions.model_answer: First, TQM prevents defects at source by making everyone responsible for quality [k]. Cross-functional teams covering assembly, testing and dispatch would find why 7% of units fail before panels are built [app]. Eliminating root causes would shrink the $180,000 rework bill and free capacity for new orders [an]. Second, TQM extends into the supply chain [k]. The supplier quality programme audits bought-in components, stopping faulty inputs reaching the test bench [app]. Fewer incoming faults raise first-pass test rates and strengthen the bid for the 8,000-panel order [an].

TQM extends quality into supplier relationships

questions.question_text: Do you think Osprey Electronics should adopt Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $85,000 over 12 months, more than the $25,000 a year of Option A, but it prevents defects at source through cross-functional teams, a suggestion scheme and supplier checks [k]. The 7% failure rate and $180,000 rework cost both point to process faults, and only TQM removes those causes rather than managing a backlog [app]. Eliminating rework quickly offsets the $85,000 programme and makes the 8,000-panel, $2 million developer order far more secure [an]. However, Option A keeps end-of-line control with overtime at $25,000 a year, cheaper immediately and clears the inspection backlog within weeks [k]. But a year of $25,000 still leaves the 7% fail rate untouched, the $180,000 rework bill standing and customer confidence flat [app]. Clearing a backlog is not the same as curing the process disease, and the developer wants evidence of reduction that inspection alone does not provide [an]. Overall, I think Osprey Electronics should adopt Option B [eval], with Option A only as a temporary supplement; the $85,000 buys prevention, the $2 million contract and falling rework costs [eval].

scenario_stem:
Thornhill Vineyards is a family-owned wine estate at its Kilmara site in Country X, producing 140,000 bottles a year from 60 hectares of vines and employing 30 staff. Wines sell at $14 a bottle, earning revenue of $1.96 million. Inconsistent fermentation means 6% of bottles are rejected at bottling, and two vintages scored poorly with critics. A supermarket chain has proposed an own-label listing worth $800,000 a year, conditional on consistent quality and an annual external audit.

The family must decide in 9 weeks. Option A: hire a full-time quality manager for $45,000 a year to run end-of-line quality control at bottling. Option B: implement winery-wide quality assurance with TQM principles, covering vine-to-bottle procedures, staff training and lab checks at each stage, costing $70,000 to set up.

questions.question_text: Define 'repeat business'.
questions.model_answer: Repeat business is when customers return to buy from the same business again, usually driven by satisfaction with the quality and service received [2].

knowledge_max_2: Customers return to buy from the same business again
Driven by satisfaction with quality and service

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why consistent quality is important for the supermarket listing at Thornhill Vineyards.
questions.model_answer: First, the supermarket listing would provide reliable, high-volume sales [k]. It is worth $800,000 a year, nearly a 41% uplift on the $1.96 million revenue, and guarantees a route to market for part of the 140,000 bottles [app]. Second, consistent quality protects reputation [k]. Two poorly scored vintages and a 6% rejection rate show how quickly standards can slip, risking withdrawal of the listing [app].

Consistent quality protects reputation and avoids losing listings

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of relying on end-of-line quality control at bottling only (Option A).
questions.model_answer: First, bottling-stage checks detect faults after they have been created [k]. Fermentation and vineyard problems arise months earlier, so rejecting faulty bottles at the end still wastes wine, glass and labour [app]. 6% of 140,000 bottles is 8,400 bottles lost every year [an]. Second, a single quality manager is a single point of failure [k]. One hire cannot continuously cover vineyard, cellar and bottling, so errors outside those hours go unchecked [app]. Poor processes persist, critic scores stay low and the supermarket may cancel the $800,000 own-label deal [an].

Reliance on one manager creates a single point of failure / limited coverage

Reference to $800,000 own-label listing / critics / end-of-line quality control

questions.question_text: Do you think Thornhill Vineyards should implement quality assurance and Total Quality Management (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B costs $70,000 once and rebuilds quality from vine to bottle, with procedures, staff training and lab checks at each stage, so fermentation faults are caught before bottling [k]. This directly targets the 6% rejection rate, 8,400 bottles a year, and gives the supermarket an audit-ready record for the $800,000 own-label listing [app]. Preventing rejects also saves wine, bottles and labour, protecting the $1.96 million revenue [an]. However, Option A hires a quality manager for $45,000 a year, $90,000 over two years, to run end-of-line checks at bottling and is simple to start within 9 weeks [k]. But it only filters faulty bottles after months of wasted work, leaves fermentation uncontrolled and does nothing for critic confidence [app]. The listing depends on an annual external audit, which a bottling-only filter cannot support [an]. Overall, I think Thornhill Vineyards should choose Option B [eval] because it removes the causes of rejects, satisfies the audit and costs less than two years of Option A [eval].
